name: Dana Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. What do you do on a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a new junior manager of four people who place sponsor spots for a large sports broadcaster. I used to run the transmission schedule myself and know which match has a youth audience and which advert contract has a restriction. I have a bachelor’s degree, but the senior managers are much better at budgets and negotiating a disputed fee. I use our approved AI checker every day to catch a wrong sponsor slot, then compare its flag with the signed agreement before the broadcast goes live.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What sits behind that job for your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner runs a small florist and our grown children live separately. We still have a mortgage and about ten months of expenses saved; I am paid above the usual junior manager rate because of my long time on transmission shifts. There are many media offices nearby, though I would have to see their actual wage. The florist takes real orders, but wedding deposits are not the same as full payment, so my salary carries the mortgage. I have not checked a retirement-income statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team AI Plateau can catch an obvious sponsor-slot mismatch, but the agreement still decides what runs beside a youth match. I would keep the signed restrictions open while we prepare the transmission list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect a modest checker to leave my new post alone. Ten months saved and my high salary give us room even when the florist has a slow week. I use the tool daily, but a contract is a promise to a sponsor and to viewers, not a pattern to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep reading the signed restrictions before approving sponsor spots and use the already approved checker to flag conflicts. I would call a producer when a youth-match label is unclear rather than let the tool decide. If the mild change arrives next year, I would keep that practice and our normal mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work in this version. I would be irritated if a green tick made us ignore a clear restriction in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a human check catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A drink advert was placed in a youth-match break because the match code had one wrong digit. The AI checker accepted a valid match code for a drink advert aimed at the wrong youth audience. I moved the spot before the producer sent the final list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch off the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It catches plenty of simple clashes, and I use it every day. I would still ask the producer to confirm what match the code actually names.

say: A **sponsor-slot check** must follow signed restrictions when the match has a youth audience.
I would keep **producer confirmation** for unclear match codes.
think: My **junior post** looks safe under a modest checker.
Ten months saved and **higher salary** buffer slow florist weeks.
do: **Keep** reading signed sponsor restrictions before spot approval.
**Use** the approved AI checker and call producers about unclear youth codes.
feel: I feel **calm** about work but irritated by false green ticks.
S0.quote: The AI checker accepted a valid match code for a drink advert aimed at the wrong youth audience.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** is established and paired with signed contracts and producer checks.
Her **ten-month reserve** and high wage buffer uneven florist receipts without turning deposits into dependable household cash.

steps.text: Keep signed sponsor restrictions open before approving transmission spots
Use approved checker and call producer about unclear youth match code

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the advertising team stronger AI will schedule spots and price routine changes faster, so some traffic jobs may go. I would publish wrong-audience placements and refunds next to the savings. A missed restriction costs a sponsor real money and can embarrass the broadcaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my new manager seat might be rolled into a bigger traffic team. I can test tools quickly, but I am still weak at the budget work that a combined manager must do. Our savings give time, and there are other media firms, but my long-service rate may be hard to match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would seek approval for a paid four-week test that compares AI placement suggestions with signed sponsor restrictions on past match schedules. I would run it only if the commercial director keeps my four staff on paid checking time and lets the producer review every wrong-audience flag. If our office merges, I would apply for posted broadcast-traffic roles only when the pay after travel and the shift rota cover our mortgage and my partner’s peak wedding weeks; I would accept only a confirmed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the manager seat even though I like improving the tool. A good test should show an expensive mistake, not just a quicker schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which past mistake would you include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sponsor bought a half-time slot, but its advert ran at the end of a delayed match when half the audience had gone. The ad software marked the half-time spot delivered even though it ran at the end of a delayed match. The sponsor asked for a credit after seeing the actual broadcast time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on staff checking time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My four people cannot check a month of past matches on their lunch breaks. If the company wants proof, it must pay for the hours and let the producer check the context. I would not call a rushed test an audit.

say: **Traffic automation** could remove scheduling posts as more sponsor spots are placed without the team.
I would publish **wrong-audience placements** and refunds beside claimed savings.
think: My **new manager seat** may merge with a larger team.
Ten months saved buys time, but **long-service pay** may be hard to replace.
do: **Request** a four-week AI placement test; run only with paid staff checks and producer review.
**Compare** past match suggestions with signed sponsor restrictions.
**Apply** for posted traffic roles only with mortgage-covering net pay and a workable wedding-season rota.
feel: I feel **anxious** about merger risk but keen to expose expensive errors.
S1.quote: The ad software marked the half-time spot delivered even though it ran at the end of a delayed match.
fieldNote: Her **AI test** uses past matches and requires commercial approval, paid staff time and producer review.
A **broadcast move** needs a posted role, verified pay, wedding-season rota and confirmed offer.

steps.text: Run four-week AI placement test only with director approval paid staff time and producer review
Compare past AI placements with signed sponsor restrictions
Apply for posted traffic role only with mortgage-covering net pay and wedding-season rota
Accept only confirmed offer after checking pay and actual shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team AGI by 2028 could place adverts, negotiate standard changes and write compliance notes before the broadcaster settles staffing or appeal rules. We would need notice and a named person who can stop a prohibited spot before it airs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think traffic teams may contract quickly, and my newer manager post could go. Sponsorship compliance is also desk work and faces 2028 AGI. Cameras and stage equipment need people for longer, until capable robots around 2031, but I am not trained as a camera operator and there is no guaranteed opening at my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask our staff council for written notice and stop-spot authority. I would compare our ten-month cash reserve with the mortgage and only count florist orders once the client has actually paid. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my post ends, I would apply to advertised local production-traffic work only with net wages after travel that cover our bills; I would accept only a real offer with shifts we can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the higher salary, but I am not without time or employers to approach. I will not tell my partner that an unbooked camera shift is a fallback wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a camera shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as if I were qualified today. I have stood in a control room for years, but that is not operating a camera on a live pitch. The physical work may change with robots around 2031, and I would need paid training and a real offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why count paid florist orders only?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wedding booking can be cancelled and a deposit returned. My partner buys flowers before receiving the final payment. We budget the money that has actually reached the shop account, not the signed date in a diary.

say: **2028 AGI** needs notice and human authority to stop prohibited adverts.
I would demand a **named appeal worker** before traffic cuts.
think: My **new traffic-manager post** could go in rapid consolidation.
Compliance desks face **2028 AGI**; physical camera work meets robots around 2031.
do: **Ask** staff council this week for notice and stop-spot authority.
**Compare** reserve with mortgage using only paid florist receipts.
**Apply** after a 2028 loss only for advertised work with bill-covering net pay and workable shifts.
feel: I feel **anxious** about higher-wage loss but able to search.
S2.quote: A wedding booking can be cancelled and a deposit returned.
fieldNote: She refuses to count **unpaid florist bookings** or unbooked camera shifts as household wages.
Her **ten-month reserve** moderates risk while all sponsorship desk roles face 2028 AGI.

steps.text: Ask staff council for written notice and prohibited-spot stop authority
Apply after loss only to posted jobs with bill-covering net pay after travel
Accept only actual offer with workable shifts and confirmed wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues five years is time to test live-event production work, but not to sell a training certificate as a camera job. I would want actual paid weekends, an experienced crew beside me and a printed rate before anyone resigns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I might enjoy running a scoreboard at a local match while I still work here. Running the scoreboard means choosing scores, timer changes and graphics, so that thinking work faces 2031 AGI too. Carrying and installing the physical display equipment meets capable robots around 2034. At 63 I would need to test late hours, and I do not know what retirement income will really be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2027 I would ask a local event company whether it has two paid match-day scoreboard shifts a month. I would accept a shift only if an actual offer names the wage, my broadcaster permits the second job, the venue supplies a trained operator to supervise and the late transport home is workable. After 2031 I would apply for an advertised production role only if pay after travel covers our mortgage and the work still exists; the trial shifts would not guarantee it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the broadcast desk, but curious about seeing a live event from the venue side. I can afford to test a paid weekend, not pretend I have a whole second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a supervisor have to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the referee’s clock stops, how to correct a wrong score without flashing an old sponsor graphic on the screen. I know the broadcast ad schedule, not how to correct a live match scoreboard. A trained operator would have to check my hands before a live crowd sees the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the florist shop cover a failed trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would not need it to cover two weekends, because I would keep my main wage. But I would not pay to work at a venue and call it a job. The trial has to be paid at an agreed rate.

say: A **five-year runway** should offer paid live-event trials and printed rates.
I would reject a **camera certificate** presented as a guaranteed job.
think: Scoreboard control and sponsor graphics face **2031 AGI**; physical equipment handling meets robots around 2034.
At **63**, late hours and retirement income remain uncertain.
do: **Ask** for paid match-day shifts from 2027; accept only with named wage, employer permission, supervisor and viable travel.
**Apply** after 2031 only for advertised production work with mortgage-covering net pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the desk but curious about live-event work.
S3.quote: I know the broadcast ad schedule, not how to correct a live match scoreboard.
fieldNote: Her **paid scoreboard shifts** require actual offers, second-job permission, supervision and safe transport.
A **production application** after 2031 needs a real vacancy and net wages; scoreboard control is exposed by then.

steps.text: Take paid scoreboard shifts only with offered wage employer permission trained supervisor and workable travel
Apply after 2031 to advertised production job only with mortgage-covering net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the broadcaster a decade is time to publish the pay for any new production roles and let staff try real event work. A sponsor paying for a live audience deserves a person who can correct the transmission, not a glossy report after the event.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I will be 68 by 2036. I may choose to stop working if our actual retirement income and savings meet the mortgage and bills, but I have not checked the entitlement or amount. Broadcast scheduling, compliance and scoreboard graphics face 2036 AGI; physical production equipment meets robots around 2039. The ten-month reserve is useful, not a permanent pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep the signed sponsor check and request an actual retirement-income statement to compare with our bills. I would add a hundred and twenty to savings only in months when my full salary and the florist’s completed payments arrive and the mortgage and shop costs are paid. After 2036 I would continue paid work if verified retirement income plus savings cannot meet our bills, and seek posted local work if broadcast shifts end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about jobs a decade ahead but secure enough to test real production work before deciding. I will not count a wedding booking twice, once as a promise and once as cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why include shop costs in the savings rule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner buys flowers and pays a shop assistant before a wedding customer settles the bill. A completed florist payment can look large until the supplier and shop assistant are paid. The extra hundred and twenty comes only from money left after those costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if retirement income is enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would check eligibility, the mortgage balance and what savings would have to cover before stopping. I have not seen the statement yet. Our grown children have their own work and should not be a line in our plan.

say: A **decade** should publish production wages and offer real event trials.
I would demand a person who can **correct live transmission**.
think: At **68**, stopping work depends on verified income, savings and bills.
Broadcast desk work faces **2036 AGI**, with physical equipment robots around 2039.
do: **Save** one hundred and twenty only after full salary, paid florist receipts, mortgage and shop costs clear.
**Continue** paid work after 2036 if verified income plus savings cannot cover bills; seek posted work if shifts end.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant jobs but able to test paid event work.
S4.quote: A completed florist payment can look large until the supplier and shop assistant are paid.
fieldNote: Her **extra saving** requires actual completed shop receipts after supplier and assistant costs, not deposits alone.
She leaves **retirement eligibility** open until verified figures show household bills can be met.
Her **broadcast income** may end by 2036 while retirement pay remains unverified, supporting anxious mood despite ten months saved.

steps.text: Keep checking signed sponsor restrictions before broadcast
Save one hundred and twenty only after full salary paid shop receipts mortgage and shop costs
Continue paid work after 2036 if verified income plus savings cannot cover bills
Seek posted local work if broadcast shifts end

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My new traffic-manager post could end before I have a paid production role, even though we have ten months saved. Written notice, stop-spot authority and real paid trials with a trained operator would help; a training advert would not be an offer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what actually aired, not only what the transmission list says. A sponsor can buy half-time and get an empty end-of-match audience. I would rather tell the sponsor the truth than celebrate a perfect software score.

headlineQuote: A sponsor can buy half-time and get an empty end-of-match audience.
portrait: **Dana, 58**, is a new junior broadcast traffic manager, learning budgets after years on transmission schedules.
Her **high long-service pay**, florist partner, ten-month reserve and many local media firms support a mortgage.
She uses **AI daily** to check sponsor slots against signed restrictions and producer context.
She is **calm** under mild change and anxious about rapid traffic cuts despite a strong cash buffer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior traffic post before paid live-production work exists.
whatWouldHelp: Written **notice**, authority to stop a prohibited spot and paid supervised trials would help.
